sections.heading: Letting you search me honestly
sections.text: All-seeing God, you know me completely. You see not only what I do, but why I do it. You know the hidden self-interest, pride, fear, and unbelief that can cling even to the things I call obedience. I can look at my obvious sins and feel ashamed, but you also see the mixed motives in my prayers, service, and worship. If even heaven is not pure before you, I have no room to defend myself. I would run from what I see in my own heart if I could.
theological_themes: God searches the heart and judges motives, not merely outward behaviour.
Even sincere religious duties can be stained by remaining sin.
True prayer begins with honest self-knowledge before God’s holiness.

scripture_references.connection: This passage presents God’s word and sight as exposing the thoughts and intentions of the heart, leaving every person fully known before him. It supports the prayer’s refusal to hide behind outward actions.

Isaiah confesses that even the righteous acts of God’s people are polluted when they stand before him in their sin. This helps ground the prayer’s concern that sin can contaminate even duties meant for God.

Job’s friend speaks of God’s purity in comparison with the heavens and human beings. While the speech in Job must be handled carefully, this particular thought reflects the biblical theme of God’s holiness exceeding all created purity.

sections.heading: Trusting the way you made for me to come back
sections.text: And yet you do not turn away from me in disgust. You have made a way for me to come home to you. You gave your Son, and he died so that I could live. In Jesus, your mercy does not ignore your justice, and your justice does not cancel your mercy. At the cross, your truth, righteousness, peace, and love are not competing with each other; they shine together.
theological_themes: God provides reconciliation for sinners through the death of his Son.
The cross upholds God’s righteousness while showing mercy to the guilty.
Salvation is God’s own gracious plan, not human self-rescue.

scripture_references.connection: Paul explains that God justifies sinners through Christ’s blood in a way that demonstrates his righteousness. This directly supports the prayer’s claim that God’s honour is not compromised but displayed in forgiving sinners.
The verse poetically joins steadfast love, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace. The prayer sees these realities coming together most fully in God’s saving work through Christ.
Jesus describes the Father’s gift of the Son as the way sinners receive life rather than condemnation. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that God has made a way back through his Son.

sections.heading: Finding everything I lack in Jesus
sections.text: In Jesus, captives are set free. The guilty are forgiven. The unclean are made new. When I am weak, he is strength that does not run out. When I am needy, he is wealth I could never measure. When I am confused and ignorant, he holds the wisdom and knowledge I need. When I am empty, he is fullness itself. I do not come to you with anything impressive in my hands. I come because Christ has everything I need.
theological_themes: Christ is sufficient for every need of salvation and spiritual life.
In Christ believers receive redemption, forgiveness, renewal, strength, wisdom, and fullness.
Human emptiness is answered by the fullness of Christ, not by self-sufficiency.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says redemption and forgiveness are found in Christ through his blood, according to God’s grace. This supports the prayer’s confidence that the enslaved and guilty find freedom and pardon in him.
This verse gathers several saving gifts in Christ: wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. It closely matches the prayer’s movement from personal lack to Christ’s complete provision.
Paul describes Christ as the one in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. This grounds the prayer’s claim that ignorance and need are met in him.
Paul teaches that the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers are filled in him. This supports the prayer’s language of fullness for the empty.

sections.heading: Receiving Christ himself, not just his gifts
sections.text: So when you call me to come, I want to come with open hands. Help me receive your grace, not reluctantly but gladly. Teach me not only to accept your mercy, but to rest in it. Let me not boast in the cross as an idea while keeping my distance from the crucified Savior. Let my joy be not only that I am forgiven, but that Jesus himself is the one who gave himself for my atonement.
theological_themes: The gospel calls sinners to come to Christ and receive grace by faith.
Faith rests gladly in God’s mercy rather than merely submitting to it with hesitation.
The believer glories not only in the benefits of the cross, but in Christ crucified.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus personally calls the weary and burdened to come to him for rest. This supports the prayer’s response to God’s gracious invitation.
John describes receiving Christ and believing in his name as the mark of those who become children of God. This grounds the prayer’s language of taking and receiving grace.
Paul’s only boast is the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ, not religious achievement or human status. This supports the prayer’s desire to glory in the crucified Savior himself.

sections.heading: Resting in what you have secured for me
sections.text: Father, the blessings you give in Christ are not fragile. You have provided for my safety, and you have promised to keep me and make me stronger. I know I cannot be truly settled without the forgiveness of my sins. I cannot be at ease while my nature remains unchanged. I cannot have deep peace without the hope of being with you forever. All of this is mine in your Son, Jesus. Blessed be his name.
theological_themes: God preserves his people and strengthens them in grace.
Forgiveness, renewal, and hope of eternal life are necessary for true peace.
All saving blessings are held together in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul expresses confidence that God will complete the good work he began in believers. This supports the prayer’s trust that God will keep and strengthen his people, not merely start their salvation.
Peter connects new birth, living hope, an imperishable inheritance, and God’s guarding power. This grounds the prayer’s peace in both present keeping and future hope.
Paul describes grace as both saving and training believers for godly lives while they wait for Christ’s appearing. This supports the prayer’s insistence that pardon and renovation belong together.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s statement that God sees more defilement in the speaker’s duties than the speaker has seen in any sins is intentionally severe. I preserved the force as a confession of mixed motives and remaining sin in acts of obedience, while avoiding the implication that sincere Spirit-enabled obedience is worthless or displeasing to God in Christ.

The allusions to Job about the heavens not being clean and angels being charged with folly come from speeches within Job, where not every statement by the speakers should be treated as straightforward doctrine without care. I used them only to echo the broader biblical theme of God’s surpassing holiness.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “acquiesce in mercy” as resting gladly in mercy, because the original means more than passive acceptance; it is a settled, consenting trust in God’s gracious way of saving.
I treated “prosperity” as spiritual flourishing and strengthening in grace, not material success, because the surrounding context is pardon, renewal, perseverance, and hope in Christ.

I kept the prayer’s movement from conviction of sin, to God’s provision in Christ, to receiving Christ himself, to assurance of final hope, rather than reorganizing it into a standard confession-assurance-thanksgiving structure.
